Disease pathology and relevance: Disruption of telomere maintenance can accelerate cellular senescence and genomic instability, processes that are increasingly implicated in β-cell failure and vascular complications in Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). The attached review directly links altered telomere biology to T2DM, suggesting that impaired telomere protection contributes to disease onset and progression.
Intersection-gene interpretation: ACD and ACTL6A participate in telomeric protein function and chromatin remodeling, while the MRE11–NBN complex monitors and repairs telomeric DNA damage, and HDAC8 can influence telomeric chromatin structure; together these genes support a mechanism where defective telomere protection and repair promote stress-induced dysfunction of metabolic cells. Their combined roles indicate that both structural telomere capping and DNA damage responses at telomeres are relevant to T2DM-associated cellular aging.
PubMed literature synthesis: The review on telomeres and maintenance genes in T2DM, along with the bioinformatics DEG study, supports a model in which altered expression of telomere-regulatory genes (including ACD, MRE11, NBN, ACTL6A, HDAC8) is enriched in T2DM and may underlie disease-related cellular senescence. The study of mesenchymal stromal cells under high glucose further suggests that hyperglycemia perturbs telomere-related pathways and regenerative capacity, linking metabolic stress to telomere dysfunction.

paragraphs: 15 submitted Type 2 diabetes mellitus-associated proteins were significantly enriched in telomere maintenance (GO:0000723).

Among the proteins enriched in this term, SIRT6, TERF2 and PRKDC represent key mechanistic links between telomere integrity and metabolic status in Type 2 diabetes mellitus. SIRT6 is a chromatin-associated deacetylase that localizes to telomeres, promotes proper telomeric chromatin structure and supports efficient repair of telomeric DNA breaks; in Type 2 diabetes mellitus it has been implicated in glucose homeostasis, insulin signaling and protection from metabolic stress–induced DNA damage, positioning it as a plausible integrator of telomere dysfunction with metabolic dysregulation. TERF2 is a core shelterin component that binds telomeric double-stranded DNA and is essential for capping chromosome ends and preventing telomere fusion; clinical and experimental studies linking shorter telomeres with Type 2 diabetes mellitus point to altered TERF2 function or regulation as a potential contributor to the telomere attrition observed in the disease. PRKDC encodes the catalytic subunit of the DNA-dependent protein kinase, a central factor in non-homologous end joining at chromosome ends and dysfunctional telomeres; in the context of Type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic hyperglycemia and oxidative stress increase DNA breakage, making PRKDC-mediated repair at telomeres a critical determinant of β-cell survival and vascular cell integrity.

The MRE11, RAD50 and NBN proteins form the a non-intersection pathway component complex, a major DNA damage sensor and processor at telomeres that detects double-strand breaks, promotes end resection and coordinates signaling to downstream repair pathways. In Type 2 diabetes mellitus, where elevated reactive oxygen species and replicative stress can accelerate telomere erosion, altered expression or function of the a non-intersection pathway component complex has been associated with impaired damage signaling and defective telomere maintenance, thereby linking these proteins to complications in highly proliferative or metabolically active tissues. Through their combined roles in sensing telomeric lesions, stabilizing stalled replication forks and facilitating appropriate repair pathway choice, the a non-intersection pathway component components provide a mechanistic bridge between the genotoxic environment of Type 2 diabetes mellitus and the telomere shortening repeatedly documented in patients.

The remaining proteins enriched in this term can be organized into functional telomere maintenance clusters that collectively shape how telomeres respond to the metabolic stresses characteristic of Type 2 diabetes mellitus. A shelterin accessory cluster comprising ACD, TERF2IP and TINF2 supports TERF2 at chromosome ends by stabilizing telomere loops, organizing telomeric chromatin and modulating access of repair factors, making these proteins key determinants of how telomeres respond to DNA damage in diabetic tissues. A non-homologous end joining cluster formed by XRCC5 and XRCC6 encodes the Ku heterodimer, which binds telomeric DNA ends and recruits PRKDC to coordinate end-joining at dysfunctional telomeres, a process that may become maladaptive when DNA breakage is increased under chronic hyperglycemia. A chromatin and transcriptional regulation cluster including ACTL6A, HDAC8 and YY1 influences nucleosome organization and epigenetic states at or near telomeres, thereby affecting telomeric gene expression programs and potentially modulating pathways such as oxidative stress responses and insulin signaling in Type 2 diabetes mellitus. Finally, RIF1 functions as a regulator of replication timing and telomere end protection, helping to control when and how telomeric DNA is replicated and repaired, which is particularly relevant in the setting of diabetes-associated replication stress.

Overall, enrichment of telomere maintenance (GO:0000723) among the proteins listed for this record indicates that coordinated regulation of telomere structure, chromatin state and DNA repair is a prominent feature of the molecular landscape of Type 2 diabetes mellitus. The association appears to be driven in particular by SIRT6, TERF2 and PRKDC, which together link metabolic control, telomere capping and DNA end-joining under conditions of chronic metabolic stress. Well-characterized interactions such as the MRE11–RAD50–NBN complex and the XRCC5–XRCC6–PRKDC non-homologous end joining assembly, as well as the cooperation of TERF2 with ACD, TERF2IP and TINF2 within shelterin, underscore that these proteins act in multi-component machines rather than in isolation. These findings support a model in which impaired telomere maintenance contributes to the cellular dysfunction and complications observed in Type 2 diabetes mellitus by integrating DNA damage, replicative stress and altered chromatin regulation at chromosome ends.

paragraphs: 141 submitted Type 2 diabetes mellitus-associated proteins were significantly enriched in regulation of transcription by RNA polymerase II (GO:0006357).

Among the most central regulators in this enrichment are the DNA methyltransferases DNMT1, DNMT3A and DNMT3B, which establish and maintain CpG methylation patterns at promoters and enhancers to modulate RNA polymerase II recruitment. In Type 2 diabetes models, altered DNMT1 and DNMT3A activity has been linked to aberrant methylation of genes controlling β‑cell identity and insulin secretion, while DNMT3B dysregulation has been associated with epigenetic changes in skeletal muscle and liver that favor insulin resistance. Collectively, these enzymes provide a stable epigenetic layer through which hyperglycaemia and metabolic stress can reprogramme transcriptional outputs in diabetes-relevant tissues.

The histone acetyltransferase EP300 acts as a transcriptional co‑activator that acetylates histones and selected transcription factors to enhance RNA polymerase II–dependent transcription. In hepatic and muscle transcriptomic studies of Type 2 diabetes, EP300 has been implicated in controlling gluconeogenic and oxidative metabolism gene sets, suggesting that its co‑activator function contributes to the transcriptional reprogramming observed in insulin-resistant states. Forkhead transcription factors FOXA1 and FOXK2, which bind nucleosomal DNA and shape chromatin accessibility, are also enriched here and have been linked to dysregulated expression of genes involved in glucose production and lipid handling in diabetic liver and muscle, reinforcing a model in which altered co‑activator–TF complexes drive pathogenic gene expression patterns.

Polycomb-group methyltransferase EZH2, together with EED, catalyses a non-intersection pathway component trimethylation at target loci to repress RNA polymerase II initiation, and this complex is increasingly implicated in β‑cell plasticity and stress responses in Type 2 diabetes. Changes in EZH2 activity have been associated with de-repression of genes that destabilize β‑cell identity and with fibrosis-related transcriptional programmes in diabetic complications. ASXL1, which cooperates with Polycomb complexes and other chromatin modifiers, is likewise enriched and has been implicated in modifying chromatin states at metabolic and inflammatory genes in experimental models of insulin resistance, consistent with a broader role for Polycomb-mediated repression in shaping the diabetic transcriptome.

Hemato-immune transcription factors BCL11A, GATA1 and GATA3 regulate lineage-specific transcription by recruiting chromatin modifiers and constraining RNA polymerase II activity at cytokine and differentiation genes. In the context of Type 2 diabetes, altered expression of these factors has been linked to skewed immune cell phenotypes and low-grade inflammation in adipose tissue and vasculature, processes that exacerbate insulin resistance and microvascular complications. The architectural transcription factor HMGA1, which binds AT‑rich DNA and bends chromatin to facilitate assembly of transcriptional complexes, is also enriched and has been associated with impaired insulin signalling gene expression in diabetic individuals, providing a direct connection between chromatin architecture and metabolic control.

Several DNA damage–responsive and chromatin-remodelling regulators with clear links to transcriptional control are also represented. BRCA1 and its partner BARD1, beyond their canonical roles in genome maintenance, modulate RNA polymerase II–dependent transcription at stress-response genes, and their dysfunction has been associated with increased oxidative stress and defective adaptive transcription in insulin-sensitive tissues under diabetic conditions. ARID2, a DNA-binding subunit of chromatin-remodelling complexes, participates in nucleosome repositioning at inducible promoters; alterations in ARID2-dependent remodelling have been connected to aberrant inflammatory and metabolic gene expression profiles reported in Type 2 diabetes transcriptome studies. Together, these factors indicate that transcription-coupled repair and remodelling pathways are integrated into the diabetic transcriptional landscape.

The remaining enriched proteins can be organized into functional clusters that converge on chromatin structure and transcriptional modulation. A Polycomb and chromatin compaction cluster includes BMI1, CBX2, CBX4, CBX5, CBX6, CBX8, EED, EHMT1, EHMT2, H1-2, H1-4, H1-5 and H2AZ1, which collectively deposit or interpret repressive histone marks and control nucleosome packing to limit RNA polymerase II access at selected loci; several have been implicated in silencing of metabolic and fibrotic genes in diabetic tissues. A nucleosome-remodelling and scaffolding cluster comprising ACTL6A, ARID4A, ARID5B, ATXN7, AUTS2, BPTF, CDK2AP1, CHD3, CHD4, EPC2 and CTBP1 regulates ATP-dependent nucleosome repositioning and corepressor assembly, consistent with the broad remodelling signatures observed in diabetic muscle and liver transcriptomes. A histone deacetylation and corepression cluster, including HDAC1, HDAC2, HDAC5, HDAC8, HDAC9, DMAP1, GATAD2A and GATAD2B, contributes to removal of acetyl marks and recruitment of repressive complexes, mechanisms linked to silencing of insulin-sensitizing genes in Type 2 diabetes models. Finally, an RNA and transcriptional cofactor cluster containing AGO1, DDX21, DEK, CBFB, HCFC1, E2F6, EYA1, FOXA1, FOXK2, GATA1, GATA3, HDGF, HMGA2 and HOXC4 integrates microRNA effector function, rRNA and mRNA processing, and sequence-specific transcriptional regulation, echoing the prominent role of post-transcriptional and transcription-factor networks in diabetic complications highlighted by microRNA and tissue transcriptome studies.

Overall, the enrichment of these proteins in regulation of transcription by RNA polymerase II underscores that Type 2 diabetes is strongly characterized by perturbations in the epigenetic and transcription-factor machinery that dictates which genes are available for transcription in metabolic and vascular tissues. The association appears to be driven primarily by broad-acting chromatin regulators such as DNMT1, EP300 and EZH2, whose activities can coordinately reprogramme large gene networks relevant to insulin secretion, insulin sensitivity and inflammation. Well-documented interactions within this set, exemplified by the formation of the EZH2–EED Polycomb complex and its cooperation with a non-intersection pathway component- and BMI1-containing Polycomb assemblies, illustrate how multiple enriched proteins physically converge to enforce repressive chromatin domains. These findings support a model in which dysregulated chromatin-based control of RNA polymerase II is a core feature of the Type 2 diabetes molecular architecture and a potential target for epigenetic intervention.

paragraphs: 95 submitted Type 2 diabetes mellitus-associated proteins were significantly enriched in negative regulation of transcription by RNA polymerase II (GO:0000122).

Among the methylation-dependent repressors enriched in this term, EZH2, EED and JARID2 exemplify Polycomb repressive complex 2 components that catalyze and interpret a non-intersection pathway component trimethylation to silence RNA polymerase II–dependent genes. In Type 2 diabetes mellitus, these proteins have been implicated in epigenetic remodeling of pancreatic islets and insulin target tissues, where altered a non-intersection pathway component methylation at metabolic and β‑cell identity genes corresponds to transcriptional repression contributing to β‑cell dysfunction and impaired glucose homeostasis. Their concurrent enrichment in this pathway suggests that Polycomb-mediated negative regulation of transcription is a prominent mechanism constraining disease-relevant gene expression programs in the TCF7L2-independent epigenetic landscape of Type 2 diabetes mellitus.

DNMT1, DNMT3A and DNMT3B represent a second axis of epigenetic repressors within this pathway, functioning as maintenance and de novo DNA methyltransferases that stabilize transcriptionally silent chromatin. In Type 2 diabetes mellitus, these enzymes have been repeatedly linked to aberrant CpG methylation at promoters and enhancers of genes controlling insulin secretion, insulin signaling and inflammatory responses, with increased methylation at specific loci corresponding to reduced transcription in pancreatic islets, adipose tissue and skeletal muscle. Their enrichment in negative regulation of RNA polymerase II–mediated transcription highlights DNA methylation–driven silencing as a core feature of the transcriptional derangements underlying the diabetic phenotype.

EP300, KAT2A, KAT2B and KAT5 jointly illustrate how histone acetyltransferases can contribute to negative regulation of transcription by dynamically modulating chromatin accessibility and cofactor recruitment at RNA polymerase II promoters. Although EP300 and its paralogs are often viewed as coactivators, in Type 2 diabetes mellitus they participate in repressive complexes and promoter-specific acetylation patterns that attenuate transcription of insulin-sensitizing and β‑cell protective genes, while favoring expression of gluconeogenic and lipogenic programs. In parallel, class I/II histone deacetylases such as HDAC1, HDAC2, HDAC5, HDAC8 and HDAC9, which remove acetyl groups from histone tails, are enriched in this term and have been linked in diabetic tissues to the repression of genes promoting insulin sensitivity and mitochondrial oxidative capacity, reinforcing acetylation-dependent transcriptional silencing in the disease context.

The remaining proteins enriched in this term can be organized into several functional clusters that converge on negative regulation of RNA polymerase II transcription in Type 2 diabetes mellitus. A Polycomb and chromatin-compaction cluster includes BMI1, CBX2, CBX4, CBX5, CBX6, CBX8 and JARID2, which bind or propagate repressive histone marks to stabilize silenced chromatin domains. A histone and DNA methylation cluster comprises EHMT1, EHMT2, KMT5A and NSD1 alongside DNMT3A and DNMT3B, coordinating repressive lysine methylation on histones with DNA methylation to shut down transcription at metabolic gene loci. A chromatin remodeling and corepressor complex cluster contains ARID4A, ARID5B, BPTF, CHD3, CHD4, CTBP1, DMAP1, GATAD2A, GATAD2B, HCFC1, MBD3, MTA1, MTA2, MTA3 and MIER3, which assemble into multisubunit complexes that reposition nucleosomes, recruit deacetylases and methyltransferases, and thereby impede RNA polymerase II initiation at diabetes-relevant promoters. A transcription factor and DNA-binding cluster features BCL11A, CBFB, CTCF, FOXA1, FOXK2, GATA1, GATA3, LEF1 and MYB, which provide sequence-specific targeting of repressive complexes to promoters and enhancers controlling β‑cell function, adipogenesis and hepatic glucose metabolism. Finally, a nuclear architecture and histone-variant cluster comprising H1-2, H1-4, H1-5, MACROH2A1, MACROH2A2, HDGF, HMGA2 and JPH2 influences higher-order chromatin structure, constraining access of RNA polymerase II to subsets of genes that modulate insulin sensitivity and inflammatory tone in Type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Overall, enrichment of these proteins in “negative regulation of transcription by RNA polymerase II” indicates that Type 2 diabetes mellitus is characterized by a substantial shift toward epigenetically enforced repression of key metabolic, stress-response and cell-identity genes. The association appears to be driven in particular by EZH2, DNMT1 and EP300, which anchor Polycomb-mediated a non-intersection pathway component methylation, DNA methylation maintenance and acetylation-dependent coregulator networks at RNA polymerase II promoters. Well-documented interactions among intersection proteins, such as the assembly of EZH2 with EED and JARID2 in Polycomb complexes, and the incorporation of CHD3, CHD4, GATAD2A, GATAD2B and MBD3 into NuRD-like deacetylase–remodeler assemblies, underscore that coordinated repressor machineries rather than isolated factors shape the diabetic transcriptional landscape. Together, these findings support a model in which multiple layers of transcriptional repression converge to lock cells into maladaptive gene expression states in Type 2 diabetes mellitus.

paragraphs: 63 submitted Type 2 diabetes mellitus-associated proteins were significantly enriched in positive regulation of transcription by RNA polymerase II (GO:0045944).

Among the enriched proteins, TCF7L2, EP300 and FOXA1 illustrate how transcriptional co-regulation may contribute to Type 2 diabetes mellitus. TCF7L2 is a key effector of Wnt-responsive transcription and functions as a DNA-binding factor that recruits co-regulators to RNA polymerase II promoters; common non-coding variants at TCF7L2 constitute one of the strongest and most consistently replicated genetic risk factors for Type 2 diabetes mellitus, primarily through effects on insulin secretion and glucose tolerance. EP300 is a histone acetyltransferase and transcriptional co-activator that acetylates histones and numerous transcription factors to enhance RNA polymerase II–mediated transcription; experimental and transcriptomic studies have linked EP300-dependent acetylation programs to β-cell gene expression, insulin secretion, and insulin sensitivity in metabolic tissues, implicating it in the pathophysiology of Type 2 diabetes mellitus. FOXA1 is a pioneer transcription factor that binds compacted chromatin and facilitates the recruitment of additional transcriptional regulators to target promoters and enhancers; in liver and other insulin-responsive tissues, FOXA1 has been shown to control transcriptional programs involved in gluconeogenesis and lipid metabolism, and dysregulation of these FOXA1-dependent networks has been associated with insulin resistance and hyperglycaemia characteristic of Type 2 diabetes mellitus.

BRCA1, KDM6A and TET1 link transcriptional activation to genomic integrity and epigenetic control in the diabetic state. BRCA1 participates in DNA damage sensing and repair and also acts as a transcriptional co-regulator at RNA polymerase II promoters; reduced BRCA1 activity has been observed in insulin-resistant and hyperglycaemic settings, where it is associated with increased oxidative DNA damage and impaired metabolic flexibility in tissues relevant to Type 2 diabetes mellitus. KDM6A is a histone demethylase that removes repressive a non-intersection pathway component methylation to activate transcription, and it has been implicated in epigenetic reprogramming of inflammatory and metabolic genes in models of obesity and Type 2 diabetes mellitus, where altered KDM6A activity contributes to sustained transcriptional activation of pathogenic gene sets. TET1 catalyses the oxidation of 5-methylcytosine and thereby facilitates active DNA demethylation, promoting transcriptional activation at specific loci; TET1-dependent DNA demethylation has been linked to the regulation of glucose- and lipid-handling genes and to β-cell functional integrity, with perturbations in TET1 activity reported in experimental systems modelling hyperglycaemia and insulin resistance.

Beyond these drivers, many of the remaining proteins enriched in this term form functional clusters that collectively support positive regulation of transcription by RNA polymerase II. A large chromatin-remodelling and histone-modifying cluster includes ARID4A, ASXL1, AUTS2, BPTF, EZH1, H2AZ1, HCFC1, HDAC1, HDAC2, HDAC5, HMGA1, HMGA2, HOXC4, KAT2A, KAT2B, KAT5, KDM1A, KDM6A, KMT2A, KMT2C, KMT2D, MTA2, PCGF5, SMARCA5, SUMO2, UHRF1, PAXIP1 and YY1; these proteins regulate nucleosome positioning, histone acetylation and methylation, higher-order chromatin architecture and co-factor recruitment, thereby modulating accessibility of RNA polymerase II to promoters of metabolic and stress-response genes that are perturbed in Type 2 diabetes mellitus. A transcription factor and co-regulator cluster comprising AGO1, BCL11A, CBFB, CTCF, EYA1, FOXK2, GATA1, GATA3, LEF1, MAML1, MEIS1, MYB, NR5A2, PBX1, RARA, RARG, RREB1, RUNX1, SIX4, SPI1, ZEB2 and HDGF provides sequence-specific DNA binding and co-activator functions that integrate hormonal, inflammatory and developmental cues into transcriptional activation programs relevant to pancreatic islets, liver, adipose tissue and skeletal muscle in the diabetic milieu. A genome maintenance and RNA-processing cluster that includes DDX21, DEK, PRKDC, TP53BP1 and XRCC6 links RNA polymerase II transcription to RNA maturation, chromatin-associated RNA metabolism and DNA damage response, processes that are increasingly recognised as altered in metabolic tissues exposed to chronic hyperglycaemia and lipotoxic stress in Type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Taken together, the enrichment of these 63 proteins in positive regulation of transcription by RNA polymerase II suggests that Type 2 diabetes mellitus involves coordinated disturbance of transcriptional activation machinery, extending from chromatin remodelling through transcription factor function to RNA and genome maintenance. Within this network, TCF7L2, EP300 and BRCA1 appear to drive the association by coupling strong genetic risk and experimentally supported metabolic phenotypes to central positions in transcriptional activation and genome surveillance. Well-documented interactions, such as cooperative activity of EP300 with sequence-specific factors including FOXA1, GATA1, GATA3 and RUNX1, and the functional interplay of BRCA1 with PRKDC, TP53BP1 and XRCC6 in DNA damage–responsive transcriptional regulation, highlight how these proteins can act in concert to shape gene expression programs in insulin-producing and insulin-responsive tissues. These findings support a model in which altered positive regulation of RNA polymerase II–dependent transcription is a core molecular feature of Type 2 diabetes mellitus, integrating genetic susceptibility with epigenetic and environmental influences on metabolic gene expression.

paragraphs: 8 submitted Type 2 diabetes mellitus-associated proteins were significantly enriched in histone deacetylase activity (GO:0004407).

Among the proteins enriched in this term, SIRT6 and HDAC1 exemplify how histone deacetylase activity can interface with metabolic control in Type 2 diabetes mellitus. SIRT6 is a nuclear, NAD+-dependent histone deacetylase that removes acetyl groups from histone lysine residues to constrain transcriptional programs involved in glucose and lipid metabolism, stress responses, and inflammation. Experimental models have shown that SIRT6 activity is critical for maintaining metabolic homeostasis, and defects in SIRT6-dependent deacetylation are linked to impaired glucose tolerance and features resembling insulin resistance, highlighting this enzyme as a plausible contributor to the epigenetic component of Type 2 diabetes mellitus. HDAC1, a prototypic class I histone deacetylase, is a core catalytic subunit of transcriptional repressor complexes that silence gene expression through deacetylation of histones at promoter regions. In the context of Type 2 diabetes mellitus, histone deacetylase activity in immune cells has been directly interrogated by pharmacological inhibition with sodium butyrate in a non-intersection pathway component-stimulated peripheral blood mononuclear cells from poorly controlled patients, underscoring that HDAC1-containing complexes are positioned to modulate inflammatory gene expression in the circulating compartment of the disease.

HDAC9 and HDAC5 further connect histone deacetylase activity to insulin-sensitive tissues that are central to Type 2 diabetes mellitus. Both belong to the class IIa subgroup of histone deacetylases, which shuttle between nucleus and cytoplasm and act primarily as transcriptional repressors by deacetylating histones and recruiting co-repressor complexes. HDAC9 has been implicated in the regulation of genes controlling muscle and vascular cell phenotype, and dysregulated HDAC9 activity has been associated with cardiometabolic traits that commonly co-occur with Type 2 diabetes mellitus. HDAC5 participates in transcriptional control of genes involved in glucose utilization and contraction-responsive signaling in skeletal muscle; altered HDAC5-regulated transcription therefore offers a mechanistic route by which epigenetic remodeling could contribute to impaired glucose uptake and insulin resistance in peripheral tissues in Type 2 diabetes mellitus.

The remaining proteins enriched in this pathway can be organized into chromatin-remodeling clusters defined by shared deacetylase-related functions. A first cluster comprises HDAC2, HDAC8, and HDAC11, all histone deacetylase catalytic subunits whose primary biochemical activity is removal of acetyl groups from lysine residues on histone tails, leading to chromatin compaction and transcriptional repression. Through this shared catalytic role, these enzymes are positioned to shape broad transcriptional programs relevant to pancreatic islet function, hepatic gluconeogenesis, and inflammatory signaling in Type 2 diabetes mellitus, even where their precise disease targets remain to be fully delineated. A second, closely allied cluster contains HDAC5, HDAC9, and the chromatin-remodeling factor MTA2, which acts as a scaffold within multi-subunit complexes that bring histone deacetylase catalytic subunits to specific genomic loci. Within this cluster, MTA2 provides targeting and structural support for deacetylase activity, enabling a non-intersection pathway component-mediated repression of gene sets whose epigenetic misregulation may contribute to the metabolic and vascular complications characteristic of Type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Taken together, enrichment of histone deacetylase activity in this analysis suggests that coordinated epigenetic control of chromatin structure is a key layer through which Type 2 diabetes mellitus–related transcriptional programs are established and maintained. Within the set of proteins listed for this record, SIRT6, HDAC1, and HDAC9 appear to be the principal drivers of the association by virtue of their direct involvement in metabolic and cardiometabolic phenotypes. Well-documented interactions among these factors, particularly the incorporation of HDAC1 and HDAC2 into MTA2-containing chromatin-remodeling complexes, indicate that histone deacetylase activity in Type 2 diabetes mellitus is exerted not by isolated enzymes but by multi-protein assemblies that couple catalytic deacetylation to selective gene targeting. These findings support a model in which altered function or regulation of specific histone deacetylase complexes contributes to the inflammatory and metabolic derangements that characterize Type 2 diabetes mellitus.

paragraphs: Exactly 20 Type 2 diabetes mellitus associated proteins were significantly enriched in the GO molecular function term “histone methyltransferase activity” (GO:0042054). This term captures enzymes that catalyze S-adenosyl-L-methionine–dependent methyl group transfer to specific lysine or arginine residues on histone proteins, thereby modifying chromatin structure and gene transcription in diabetes-relevant tissues.

Among the lysine methyltransferases, KMT2A, KMT2C and KMT2D are notable because they catalyze methylation of histone tails at regulatory regions to promote transcription of target genes involved in differentiation and metabolism. KMT2A is of particular interest, as its encoded histone methyltransferase has been directly implicated in macrophage-mediated inflammation during wound healing and shown to be altered in a murine model of obesity and Type 2 diabetes, linking this pathway to inflammatory complications and impaired tissue repair in the diabetic state. KMT2C and KMT2D participate in related chromatin-activating complexes in metabolic tissues, where they are positioned to influence transcriptional programs underlying adipocyte differentiation, hepatic glucose handling and systemic insulin sensitivity, consistent with epigenetic studies in Type 2 diabetes that highlight dysregulated activation of metabolic gene networks.

The polycomb-related enzymes EZH1 and EZH2, together with the accessory factor JARID2, constitute another key axis within this enriched set. EZH2 and its paralog EZH1 catalyze methylation at repressive histone sites within polycomb complexes, thereby silencing developmental and metabolic genes; in the context of Type 2 diabetes, altered polycomb-mediated repression has been linked to persistent changes in gene expression in pancreatic islets, vascular cells and immune cells that contribute to β-cell dysfunction, endothelial injury and low-grade inflammation. JARID2 functions as a recruitment and regulatory subunit for these complexes, guiding EZH1/EZH2 to specific genomic loci; epigenetic work in diabetes and its complications indicates that such targeting mechanisms are critical for establishing long-lasting repressive chromatin states in response to hyperglycemia and metabolic stress.

Another prominent subgroup consists of enzymes that deposit methyl marks associated with transcriptional repression in heterochromatin or at repeated sequences. EHMT1 and EHMT2 catalyze methylation on lysine residues within euchromatin, enforcing silencing of gene sets that include regulators of gluconeogenesis, adipogenesis and inflammation, and they have been functionally linked to insulin resistance and lipid accumulation in experimental models of metabolic disease. SUV39H1 and KMT5A further consolidate repressive chromatin, with SUV39H1 acting predominantly at heterochromatic regions and KMT5A establishing mono-methyl marks required for higher-order chromatin compaction; epigenetic analyses in Type 2 diabetes and obesity have connected such repressive modifications with aberrant silencing of genes that normally restrain oxidative stress, fibrosis and vascular pathology in diabetic complications.

The remaining enriched proteins can be organized into clusters with related biochemical functions. NSD1 and NSD2 form a cluster of lysine methyltransferases that act in gene bodies and regulatory elements to modulate transcriptional elongation and chromatin accessibility in metabolic tissues. PRMT1, PRMT5 and PRMT6 constitute a group of protein arginine methyltransferases that symmetrically or asymmetrically methylate arginine residues on histones and non-histone substrates, thereby intersecting histone methylation with insulin signaling pathways and inflammatory cascades implicated in Type 2 diabetes. SETD1A and SETDB1 represent a pair of enzymes with opposing influences on chromatin activity, with SETD1A contributing to transcriptionally active chromatin at metabolic and cell-cycle genes and SETDB1 enforcing repressive methylation in regions linked to immune regulation and stress responses. KMT2B, closely related to KMT2A/C/D, collaborates with WDR5, a core scaffolding protein in multiple lysine methyltransferase complexes, and with the regulatory factor SETBP1 to stabilize and target activating methyltransferase assemblies to specific promoters and enhancers; collectively, these proteins help define the chromatin landscape that underlies durable transcriptional reprogramming in insulin resistance and diabetic end-organ damage.

Overall, enrichment of these 20 proteins in histone methyltransferase activity underscores that aberrant chromatin methylation is a central axis through which genetic and environmental risk factors converge in Type 2 diabetes mellitus. The association appears to be driven in particular by KMT2A, which has direct experimental support in a murine model of obesity and diabetes, together with EZH2 and PRMT5 as key effectors at the interface of transcriptional control, inflammation and metabolic stress. Well-documented physical and functional interactions among intersection proteins, such as those between KMT2A family members and WDR5 in activating methyltransferase complexes and between EZH1/EZH2 and JARID2 in polycomb assemblies, indicate that they act not as isolated enzymes but as coordinated modules. These findings support a model in which combinatorial histone methylation, rather than single-gene effects, shapes the persistent epigenetic alterations characteristic of Type 2 diabetes and its complications.

Among the proteins enriched in this term, EP300 stands out as a versatile lysine acetyltransferase that directly catalyses transfer of acetyl groups from acetyl-CoA to specific histone lysine residues, thereby modulating chromatin accessibility in cells relevant to metabolic homeostasis. KAT2A is another catalytic histone acetyltransferase enriched in this pathway, and its presence alongside EP300 within the Type 2 diabetes mellitus protein set highlights a convergence on transcriptional co‑activation mechanisms that can integrate nutrient and stress signals at the chromatin level.

KAT5 represents a further core effector of histone acetyltransferase activity in this intersection, catalysing acetylation of histones within multi-subunit nuclear complexes and linking acetyl-CoA utilization to regulation of gene expression programs that are perturbed in Type 2 diabetes mellitus. Within the context of this pathway enrichment, the combined presence of EP300, KAT2A and KAT5 suggests that multiple enzymatic nodes of histone lysine acetylation contribute to the chromatin remodeling capacity embedded in the submitted Type 2 diabetes mellitus module.

The remaining enriched proteins can be grouped into auxiliary histone acetyltransferase components and specialized acetyltransferases. JADE2 and MEAF6 function as regulatory subunits within histone acetyltransferase complexes, supporting substrate recognition, complex stability and targeting of acetyltransferase activity to defined genomic regions, and thereby modulating the output of the catalytic subunits captured in this pathway. HAT1, in contrast, is a more specialized acetyltransferase that preferentially acetylates newly synthesized histone H4, linking histone supply and deposition to the acetylation-dependent chromatin landscape represented in this Type 2 diabetes mellitus-associated set, while KAT2B provides additional a non-intersection pathway component/a non-intersection pathway component-family acetyltransferase activity that complements KAT2A-driven acetylation.

Overall, enrichment of these 7 proteins in the histone acetyltransferase activity pathway indicates that acetyl-CoA–dependent modification of histone lysine residues is a prominent molecular function within the Type 2 diabetes mellitus protein module. EP300, KAT2A and KAT5 appear to be the principal drivers of this association, as they provide the core catalytic activities around which the other intersection proteins are organized. Interactions among KAT5, JADE2 and MEAF6 within shared acetyltransferase complexes exemplify how catalytic and regulatory subunits cooperate to shape chromatin acetylation states, providing a mechanistic scaffold through which histone acetyltransferase activity can influence gene regulation in Type 2 diabetes mellitus.

paragraphs: Exactly 28 Type 2 diabetes mellitus associated proteins were significantly enriched in the GO molecular function term “histone binding” (GO:0042393).

Among the histone-binding proteins, EZH2, EZH1 and WDR5 stand out as central epigenetic regulators with direct relevance to Type 2 diabetes mellitus. EZH2 and its paralog EZH1 are histone methyltransferase subunits that bind nucleosomal histones to catalyze methylation of histone H3, thereby enforcing repressive chromatin states at metabolic and stress-responsive loci. Epigenetic reviews in metabolic disease have implicated EZH2-mediated histone methylation in the transcriptional adaptation of insulin target tissues to nutrient excess and inflammation, suggesting that aberrant EZH2/EZH1 activity contributes to insulin resistance and altered mitochondrial energetics in Type 2 diabetes mellitus. WDR5 is a WD-repeat scaffold that binds the histone H3 tail and organizes histone methyltransferase complexes at chromatin, and has been linked to epigenetic programming of energy metabolism and endocrine function in diabetes-related contexts, positioning WDR5 as a key coordinator of histone-binding methyltransferase activity in the diabetic epigenome.

HDAC2, PRMT6 and UHRF1 represent a second group of notable histone-binding regulators that converge on chromatin modifications relevant to diabetic tissue injury. HDAC2 is a class I histone deacetylase that engages nucleosomal histones to remove acetyl groups, and epigenetic studies in metabolic disease indicate that HDAC2-dependent deacetylation modulates inflammatory and oxidative-stress pathways that are exacerbated in Type 2 diabetes mellitus, consistent with reports that targeting histone acetylation can ameliorate diabetes-induced vascular and cognitive complications. PRMT6 is a protein arginine methyltransferase that binds histones to deposit asymmetric arginine methyl marks, and has been implicated in shaping transcriptional responses to nutrient status and gut microbiota–derived metabolites in metabolic disease models, linking histone arginine methylation to insulin sensitivity and systemic glucose handling. UHRF1 is a multifunctional chromatin factor that recognizes histone tails and couples histone marks to DNA methylation maintenance; in the diabetic setting, altered UHRF1-mediated crosstalk between histone binding and DNA methylation has been associated with persistent epigenetic “memory” of hyperglycemia in target organs such as the kidney and vasculature.

The remaining enriched histone-binding proteins fall into several functional clusters. A Polycomb and related chromatin repression cluster includes PHC1, PHC2, PHC3, RBBP4, RBBP5, RBBP7, L3MBTL3 and SFMBT1, which cooperate with core methyltransferase subunits to bind histones and maintain silenced chromatin domains, a mechanism repeatedly implicated in long-term epigenetic remodeling of metabolic and inflammatory genes in Type 2 diabetes mellitus. A chromatin-remodeling cluster, comprising CHD3, CHD4, SMARCA5 and DEK, binds histones within nucleosomes to reposition or restructure chromatin, supporting diabetes-related changes in accessibility at genes controlling mitochondrial function, oxidative stress and cardiomyocyte energetics. A histone-chaperone and modification-assembly cluster, including ASF1A and HAT1 together with the core histones H2AX and H2BC1, underpins nucleosome assembly and acetylation states that influence susceptibility to diabetes-induced oxidative damage, as illustrated by studies of histone lactylation and cognitive impairment in experimental diabetes. Finally, a DNA damage signaling and repair cluster—NBN, RNF8, TP53BP1, UIMC1, USP3 and USP49—relies on specific binding to modified histones (notably phosphorylated H2AX) to coordinate repair of oxidative and replication-associated DNA lesions, a pathway that is activated in hyperglycemic tissues and in diabetic cardiomyopathy.

paragraphs: 35 submitted Type 2 diabetes mellitus-associated proteins were significantly enriched in histone deacetylase complex (GO:0000118).

Among the enriched proteins, HDAC1 and HDAC2 are catalytic class I histone deacetylases that form the enzymatic core of several nuclear corepressor complexes. In the context of Type 2 diabetes mellitus, both have been implicated in epigenetic repression of genes governing insulin sensitivity and β‑cell function, and they are prominent components of nuclear receptor corepressor assemblies that modulate the peroxisome proliferator‑activated receptor gamma axis highlighted in the attached literature. SIN3A acts as a scaffold within one of the canonical HDAC1/HDAC2 complexes, integrating these deacetylases with additional chromatin‑binding subunits; in metabolic tissues, SIN3A‑containing complexes have been reported to participate in transcriptional programs that affect glucose homeostasis and insulin signaling.

Class II and other non–class I deacetylases are also represented, with HDAC5, HDAC8, HDAC9 and HDAC11 providing additional enzymatic activities within histone deacetylase assemblies. HDAC5 and HDAC9 shuttle between cytoplasm and nucleus and, when incorporated into nuclear complexes, can repress transcriptional regulators that are important for insulin responsiveness in muscle and adipose tissue, again aligning with a role in nuclear receptor corepression. HDAC8 and HDAC11 contribute further deacetylase capacity to these complexes, and their recruitment to chromatin has been linked to changes in expression of metabolic genes relevant to Type 2 diabetes mellitus, although their disease associations appear less extensively characterized than those of HDAC1/HDAC2 and HDAC5. Beyond deacetylation per se, chromatin‑modifying enzymes such as JMJD1C (histone lysine demethylase), TET1 (DNA demethylase), KAT5 (histone acetyltransferase) and KMT2E (histone methyltransferase) also enter a non-intersection pathway component‑containing assemblies; these proteins have been implicated in epigenetic remodeling of loci that control adipogenesis, inflammation and insulin action, supporting a broader link between dynamic chromatin modification and Type 2 diabetes mellitus risk.

The histone deacetylase complex term from the cellular component ontology captures nuclear, chromatin‑associated multiprotein complexes in which these enzymes and cofactors reside, rather than specifying the particular transcriptional programs they regulate. Within this compartment, several proteins, including RBBP4, RBBP7, SIN3B, SAP18, SAP30, MTA1, MTA2 and MTA3, act as relatively stable structural scaffolds or adaptor subunits, helping to organize canonical a non-intersection pathway component‑ and NuRD‑like complexes around the a non-intersection pathway component catalytic cores. Chromatin‑remodeling ATPase components such as CHD3 and CHD4, together with associated factors GATAD2A, GATAD2B, MBD3, DMAP1, MORF4L1, RCOR1, PHF21A, SINHCAF, ARID4A and CDK2AP1, form a second functional cluster that remodels nucleosome positioning and DNA accessibility in proximity to a non-intersection pathway component activity. A third cluster comprises chromatin readers and transcription‑linked cofactors, including CBX5, EP400, TRRAP and ZNF217, which can be transient residents of a non-intersection pathway component complexes, targeting them to specific genomic regions or integrating acetylation and deacetylation signals. These groupings indicate that the enriched proteins co‑localize within nuclear deacetylase assemblies, but this co‑localization alone does not establish that they act through a single shared mechanism in Type 2 diabetes mellitus; some are core structural constituents, whereas others likely cycle on and off the complexes depending on cellular state.

Taken together, the enrichment of these 35 proteins in the histone deacetylase complex pathway suggests that nuclear deacetylase‑centered chromatin assemblies are an important locus of Type 2 diabetes mellitus–related molecular variation. The association appears to be driven most strongly by the core catalytic and scaffolding components HDAC1, HDAC5 and SIN3A, which participate in nuclear receptor corepressor complexes that influence transcriptional responses relevant to insulin sensitivity. Well‑documented physical interactions among intersection proteins, such as those between HDAC1/HDAC2, SIN3A, RBBP4/RBBP7 and SAP18/SAP30 within a non-intersection pathway component complexes, and between CHD3/CHD4 and GATAD2A/GATAD2B/MBD3 within NuRD‑like assemblies, indicate that multiple interacting a non-intersection pathway component‑containing complexes underlie this signal. These observations support a model in which altered composition or function of histone deacetylase complexes contributes to the epigenetic component of Type 2 diabetes mellitus pathophysiology, without implying that all enriched proteins converge on an identical molecular mechanism.

paragraphs: 259 submitted Type 2 diabetes mellitus-associated proteins were significantly enriched in nucleus (GO:0005634).

The proteins listed for this record are therefore enriched in a membrane-bounded compartment that houses the chromosomes and supports nuclear RNA synthesis and processing, but GO:0005634 itself specifies localization rather than mechanism. Within this compartment, several of the Type 2 diabetes mellitus associated proteins, such as DNMT1, DNMT3A and DNMT3B, are stable, chromatin-bound enzymes that help define long-lived epigenetic states, whereas others are more transient residents that shuttle between the nucleus and cytoplasm in response to metabolic or circadian cues. The nucleus is a critical site at which hyperglycaemia, oxidative stress and altered hormonal signaling can be translated into durable changes in gene expression, but co-localization of these proteins in the nucleus is not, by itself, evidence that they act in a single shared pathway or mechanism in Type 2 diabetes mellitus.

DNMT1, DNMT3A and DNMT3B are nuclear DNA methyltransferases that establish and maintain cytosine methylation patterns across the genome, thereby linking environmental inputs to long-term transcriptional programs. Experimental and human studies have implicated altered DNA methylation in pancreatic islets, liver and other insulin-responsive tissues in the pathogenesis of Type 2 diabetes mellitus, and genetic or acquired variation in DNMT1, DNMT3A and DNMT3B has been associated with abnormal methylation at loci controlling insulin secretion, circadian regulation of metabolism and hypothalamic energy balance. Within the nucleus, these enzymes act as catalytic cores that can integrate signals arising from obesity, disrupted circadian clocks and hypothalamic dysregulation, converting them into epigenetic marks that may contribute to persistent insulin resistance and β-cell dysfunction in Type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Among histone-modifying and transcriptional co-regulatory proteins enriched in the nucleus, EP300 functions as a histone acetyltransferase and transcriptional co-activator that acetylates histones and non-histone substrates to promote open chromatin and active transcription. Nuclear EP300 activity has been linked to regulation of genes involved in gluconeogenesis, lipid handling and circadian clock output, and altered EP300 function has been reported in models of insulin resistance and Type 2 diabetes mellitus, consistent with a role in reshaping transcriptional programs in hepatic and hypothalamic nuclei under diabetic conditions. The histone methyltransferase EZH2, together with its paralog EZH1, catalyzes repressive a non-intersection pathway component methylation in nuclear Polycomb complexes; EZH2 has been implicated in aberrant silencing of genes controlling adipogenesis, inflammatory signaling and β-cell survival in Type 2 diabetes mellitus, suggesting that nuclear accumulation of this enzyme contributes to maladaptive repression of metabolic and neuroendocrine pathways. BRCA1, a nuclear protein best known for its role in DNA damage repair, has also been associated with oxidative-stress responses in metabolically active tissues, and experimental perturbation of nuclear BRCA1 complexes has been linked to altered insulin signaling and mitochondrial function in the context of Type 2 diabetes mellitus.

A broader set of nuclear proteins enriched in this term can be organized into functional clusters. A first cluster comprises Polycomb-group and related chromatin methylation modules, including BMI1, CBX2, CBX4, CBX6, CBX8, EED, EZH1, EZH2, ASH2L and DPY30, which assemble into multi-subunit complexes that deposit or interpret histone methylation marks to maintain repressed or active transcriptional states at developmental and metabolic loci; altered activity of such complexes in hypothalamic and peripheral nuclei is consistent with persistent reprogramming of appetite and energy-homeostasis circuits in Type 2 diabetes mellitus. A second cluster contains chromatin-remodeling factors and histone chaperones, such as ACTL6A, CHD3, CHD4, BPTF, ASF1A, CHAF1A, EP400, EPC2 and DMAP1, which restructure nucleosomes or assist histone exchange to regulate access of transcriptional and DNA repair machineries, providing a nuclear interface through which diabetic oxidative stress and glucotoxicity can influence genome stability and gene expression. A third cluster includes DNA damage–response and genome-stability proteins, including BRCA1, BARD1, BRCC3, CHEK2, BABAM2, BAP1, ETAA1, EMSY, ACD and CDK2AP1, whose nuclear functions in sensing and repairing DNA lesions are relevant in the setting of increased oxidative and replicative stress reported in Type 2 diabetes mellitus. Additional clusters encompass nuclear transcriptional regulators and co-regulators such as ARID2, ARID4A, ARID5B, CTBP1, CTCF, E2F6, BCL11A, CBFB, DEK, EYA1, EYA2, AUTS2 and ATXN7; RNA-processing and nuclear a non-intersection pathway component-associated proteins including AGO1, AGO3, AGO4, DDX21, CWF19L1 and DDI2; and signaling or enzymatic factors with nuclear pools, such as DGKD, CAMKMT, EHMT1, EHMT2, CBX1, CBX3 and CBX5, all of which provide additional routes through which diabetic metabolic and circadian perturbations can be encoded within nuclear regulatory networks.

Overall, enrichment of Type 2 diabetes mellitus associated proteins in the nucleus pathway suggests that a substantial fraction of the genetic and molecular perturbations implicated in this disease converge on nuclear compartments where chromatin structure, DNA integrity and transcriptional programs are coordinated. Within this localization context, DNMT1, DNMT3A and DNMT3B appear to be key drivers of the association, because of their central roles in shaping nuclear DNA methylation landscapes that are repeatedly linked to diabetic phenotypes. Well-characterized nuclear interactions among intersection proteins, such as the formation of BRCA1–BARD1–BRCC3 complexes in DNA repair and the assembly of EZH2 with EED and a non-intersection pathway component proteins in Polycomb repressive complexes, illustrate that many of these factors act in multi-protein assemblies rather than in isolation. Although their co-localization to the nucleus does not in itself prove a single shared mechanism, it supports the view that nuclear epigenetic regulation and genome maintenance are major points of integration for the diverse metabolic, circadian and hypothalamic signals that contribute to Type 2 diabetes mellitus pathology.

paragraphs: 27 submitted Type 2 diabetes mellitus-associated proteins were significantly enriched in histone methyltransferase complex (GO:0035097).

Within these complexes, EZH2 acts as a catalytic subunit of a Polycomb histone methyltransferase that deposits repressive methyl marks on histone tails, thereby compacting chromatin and limiting transcription. Epigenetic studies in human islets and pharmaco-epigenetic work in Type 2 diabetes support a role for such repressive histone methyltransferase activities in controlling β-cell gene expression, insulin secretory capacity, and potentially the epigenetic responsiveness of islet cells to anti-diabetic therapies, making EZH2 a plausible contributor to the observed enrichment. KMT2D is a large a non-intersection pathway component methyltransferase that generates activating histone marks at enhancers, and genetic syndromes caused by mutations in epigenetic genes highlight KMT2D as a central regulator of developmental and metabolic transcriptional programs; its presence in this enriched set is consistent with reports that altered histone methylation at key metabolic loci is a feature of Type 2 diabetes. PRMT5, a histone arginine methyltransferase enriched in the same complexes, symmetrically dimethylates arginine residues and thereby modulates chromatin accessibility; epigenetic analyses in diabetic tissues and islets implicate arginine as well as lysine methylation in shaping the transcriptional response to hyperglycemia and insulin resistance, suggesting that PRMT5-mediated chromatin remodeling is relevant to disease-associated transcriptional reprogramming.

Several additional proteins in the intersection form the core of activating a non-intersection pathway component methyltransferase assemblies. KMT2A, KMT2B and KMT2C are large catalytic subunits that, together with SETD1A, deposit a non-intersection pathway component methylation at promoters and enhancers, while ASH2L, WDR5, RBBP5 and DPY30 provide structural scaffolding and cofactor-binding functions that stabilize the catalytic centers and couple methyltransferase activity to transcriptional machinery. Transcriptional and epigenetic profiling of human islets in Type 2 diabetes demonstrates widespread remodeling of active chromatin at genes controlling insulin synthesis, secretion and stress responses, and the enrichment of these core a non-intersection pathway component complex constituents suggests that altered assembly or targeting of such activating methyltransferase complexes contributes to the diabetic islet transcriptional state.

A second functionally coherent group comprises Polycomb-related and associated chromatin regulators embedded within histone methyltransferase complexes. EZH1 provides catalytic activity overlapping with EZH2 in repressive complexes, while EED and SUZ12 are structural subunits required for complex integrity and allosteric activation, and JARID2 and PHF1 act as accessory factors that guide complex recruitment and modulate substrate specificity. Together, these proteins localize to nuclear chromatin regions where they establish or maintain repressive histone methylation, and epigenetic work in Type 2 diabetes and in genetic syndromes caused by epigenetic-gene mutations indicates that disruption of such Polycomb-mediated repression can perturb metabolic gene networks and stress-response pathways in insulin-producing and insulin-responsive tissues.

The remaining proteins enriched in this cellular component term belong to several related chromatin-regulatory clusters. One cluster comprises additional scaffolding and histone-binding proteins, including RBBP4 and RBBP7, which link methyltransferase complexes to nucleosomes, and CBX5 and RNF2, which recognize and enforce repressive chromatin states within higher-order assemblies. A second cluster is formed by transcriptional cofactors and complex-adaptor proteins such as HCFC1, PAXIP1 and PHF3, which help tether histone methyltransferase complexes to specific genomic regions in response to transcriptional cues. A third group encompasses HDAC2 and HDAC9, histone deacetylases that co-localize with methyltransferase complexes on chromatin, as well as KDM6A, a demethylase that counteracts repressive marks; these are best viewed as transient functional partners rather than structural subunits of histone methyltransferase complexes. Collectively, these proteins reside predominantly in the nuclear chromatin compartment rather than a classical organelle, and while this shared localization indicates co-residence in histone-modifying assemblies that are relevant to Type 2 diabetes epigenetic regulation, such co-localization alone does not constitute evidence that all intersection proteins participate in a single, unified pathogenic mechanism.

Overall, enrichment of these 27 Type 2 diabetes mellitus associated proteins in the histone methyltransferase complex term indicates that nuclear chromatin-modifying assemblies are a prominent subcellular context in which genetic and epigenetic risk converges in this disease. The pattern of intersection proteins points to EZH2, KMT2D and PRMT5 as key drivers of the association, reflecting the combined importance of repressive and activating lysine methylation and arginine methylation in shaping diabetes-related transcriptional programs. Well-documented physical and functional interactions among components such as a non-intersection pathway component family enzymes with ASH2L–WDR5–RBBP5–DPY30 core subunits, and between EZH1/EZH2 and EED–SUZ12–JARID2 within Polycomb complexes, underscore that these proteins act in tightly organized assemblies whose dysregulation can plausibly reconfigure chromatin states in Type 2 diabetes relevant tissues. Thus, this pathway highlights histone methyltransferase complexes as central nuclear platforms through which epigenetic mechanisms may influence disease susceptibility and progression.

paragraphs: 13 submitted Type 2 diabetes mellitus-associated proteins were significantly enriched in NuRD complex (GO:0016581).

CHD4 and CHD3 are ATP-dependent chromatin-remodeling ATPases that form the Mi-2–like core of the NuRD complex within the nucleus, where they act on nucleosomal DNA to modulate chromatin accessibility. The attached literature indicates that the CHD4 subunit regulates Pdx1-controlled genes involved in beta-cell function and that CHD3 and CHD4 jointly coordinate gene expression programs required to maintain beta-cell function and identity in vivo, linking these remodelers directly to cellular processes that are disrupted in Type 2 diabetes mellitus. Because these proteins are enriched in a nuclear chromatin-remodeling complex rather than in a discrete pathological structure, their contribution to disease is mediated through transcriptional control rather than a localized structural lesion, and their co-localization within NuRD should not be taken as evidence that they act through a single, uniform mechanism in all contexts.

HDAC1 and HDAC2 are class I histone deacetylases that constitute the catalytic deacetylase core of the NuRD complex, where they remove acetyl groups from histone tails to promote transcriptional repression. NuRD has been reported to mediate transcriptional control of gluconeogenic genes in the context of systemic glucose homeostasis, implicating HDAC1- and HDAC2-containing NuRD assemblies in the regulation of hepatic gluconeogenesis that is characteristically dysregulated in Type 2 diabetes mellitus. Within this nuclear complex, HDAC1 and HDAC2 are structural constituents of the chromatin-bound machinery rather than transient visitors, but their enrichment in NuRD again reflects shared subcellular localization and complex membership rather than proving that they influence diabetes risk through a single shared downstream pathway.

The remaining enriched proteins can be organized into functional clusters based on their roles within the NuRD holocomplex. A first cluster comprises the MTA1, MTA2 and MTA3 proteins together with the histone-binding proteins RBBP4 and RBBP7, which form a scaffolded histone-recognition module that stabilizes the complex on nucleosomes and helps couple the CHD3/CHD4 ATPases to HDAC1/HDAC2-mediated deacetylation during transcriptional repression at beta-cell and gluconeogenic target genes. A second, more regulatory cluster includes GATAD2A, GATAD2B, MBD3, HDAC2 and CDK2AP1, which together bridge DNA- and chromatin-reading activities to the remodeling and deacetylase core, thereby modulating where and when NuRD is deployed on the genome in tissues relevant to Type 2 diabetes mellitus. All of these proteins are structural constituents of the nuclear NuRD complex, and their enrichment indicates shared complex membership and chromatin localization, but—consistent with the nature of GO Cellular Component terms—this co-localization alone does not demonstrate that each subunit contributes to diabetes through the same mechanistic route.

paragraphs: 7 submitted Type 2 diabetes mellitus-associated proteins were significantly enriched in SUMOylation of transcription factors (REAC:R-HSA-3232118).

Among the proteins enriched in this term, UBE2I functions as the central a non-intersection pathway component-conjugating E2 enzyme that transfers activated a non-intersection pathway component moieties to lysine residues on transcription factor substrates. Within the SUMOylation of transcription factors pathway, UBE2I acts as a catalyst that receives SUMO1, SUMO2 or SUMO3 from the E1 activating complex and, together with pathway-specific E3 ligases, catalyzes their covalent attachment to transcription factors that govern adipocyte differentiation and insulin sensitivity, as highlighted in studies of covalent modifications of nuclear receptors. By modulating the SUMOylation status of such transcriptional regulators, UBE2I has been implicated in the fine-tuning of metabolic gene programs that underpin insulin responsiveness and systemic metabolic homeostasis in Type 2 diabetes mellitus.

PIAS4 serves as a a non-intersection pathway component E3 ligase within this pathway, functioning as a catalyst that bridges UBE2I–a non-intersection pathway component thioester intermediates to specific transcription factor substrates. In the Reactome event chain, PIAS4 operates in the ligation step immediately downstream of a non-intersection pathway component activation and transfer to UBE2I, thereby conferring target specificity to the SUMOylation of transcription factors controlling adipocyte development and inflammatory responses relevant to insulin resistance. Experimental work on covalent modifications of key adipogenic transcription factors indicates that a non-intersection pathway component-family E3 ligases, including PIAS4, can influence their transcriptional output, providing a mechanistic link between PIAS4-dependent SUMOylation and altered insulin sensitivity in Type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Within the same pathway, SUMO1, SUMO2 and SUMO3 act as ubiquitin-like modifiers that are both substrates and products of successive SUMOylation reactions. They are first activated by the upstream E1 machinery, then passed to UBE2I, and finally conjugated to transcription factors in reactions catalyzed by PIAS4; in Reactome, these steps appear as a series of linked reactions in which SUMO1, SUMO2 and SUMO3 participate alongside the catalytic components rather than within a single reaction step. The attached literature on transcription factor acetylation and post-translational modification of adipogenic regulators indicates that a non-intersection pathway component paralogs can repress or redirect transcription factor activity controlling lipid storage and insulin action, situating SUMO1, SUMO2 and SUMO3 as direct molecular mediators of transcriptional reprogramming observed in Type 2 diabetes mellitus.

The remaining enriched proteins in this pathway can be grouped into two functional clusters. A chromatin-associated regulator cluster comprises MTA1 and TP53BP1, which are annotated in Reactome as transcriptional regulators that become SUMOylated substrates within this pathway, entering at the terminal modification steps downstream of UBE2I- and PIAS4-catalyzed conjugation. SUMOylation of such chromatin-associated factors has been reported to modulate the transcriptional activity of metabolic regulators described in the attached literature, suggesting that MTA1 and TP53BP1 participate in a non-intersection pathway component-dependent remodeling of transcriptional networks relevant to glucose and lipid metabolism in Type 2 diabetes mellitus. A a non-intersection pathway component-paralog cluster, encompassing SUMO2 and SUMO3, provides alternative conjugated modifiers whose dynamic cycling on transcription factors can differentially influence the same metabolic gene programs governed by SUMO1, in keeping with the broader evidence that distinct a non-intersection pathway component isoforms fine-tune nuclear receptor–driven control of adipocyte development and insulin sensitivity.

Taken together, enrichment of UBE2I, PIAS4, SUMO1, SUMO2, SUMO3, MTA1 and TP53BP1 in the “SUMOylation of transcription factors” pathway indicates that dysregulated a non-intersection pathway component conjugation of transcriptional regulators is a prominent axis linking post-translational modification to altered gene expression in Type 2 diabetes mellitus. The association appears to be driven primarily by the core SUMOylation machinery components UBE2I, PIAS4 and SUMO1, which orchestrate the conjugation of a non-intersection pathway component paralogs to transcription factors that control adipocyte development and insulin sensitivity. Within this pathway, UBE2I and PIAS4 interact directly through the canonical E2–E3 enzyme pairing, while SUMO1, SUMO2 and SUMO3 form transient conjugates with MTA1 and TP53BP1 in successive reaction steps, collectively supporting a model in which coordinated SUMOylation of chromatin-associated transcriptional regulators contributes to the transcriptional dysregulation characteristic of Type 2 diabetes mellitus.

paragraphs: 167 submitted Type 2 diabetes mellitus-associated proteins were significantly enriched in chromatin organization (GO:0006325).

Among the proteins enriched in this term, EP300, CTCF and FOXA1 exemplify how altered higher-order chromatin structure may contribute to Type 2 diabetes mellitus. EP300 is a histone acetyltransferase and transcriptional co-activator that deposits activating acetyl marks at enhancers and promoters, and pancreatic islet multiome and 3D chromatin mapping studies have implicated EP300-bound regulatory elements at loci harboring Type 2 diabetes risk variants, consistent with a role in modulating beta cell gene expression programs in disease. CTCF functions as a chromatin insulator and architectural protein that anchors loop boundaries and topologically associating domains, and pancreas-focused 3D chromatin maps indicate that CTCF-occupied sites participate in lineage-specific regulatory architectures that are perturbed at Type 2 diabetes risk regions, suggesting that changes in CTCF-mediated genome topology can influence beta cell susceptibility. FOXA1 is a pioneer transcription factor that binds compacted chromatin and facilitates nucleosome displacement, and single-cell multiome profiling of pancreatic islets has linked altered FOXA1 motif accessibility and occupancy to diabetes-related changes in cell type–specific regulatory programs, supporting a model in which FOXA1-dependent chromatin opening contributes to disease-relevant transcriptional states.

A second set of notable proteins links histone and DNA methylation to Type 2 diabetes mellitus. EZH2 is the catalytic subunit of the a non-intersection pathway component complex that tri-methylates histone H3 on lysine 27 to establish repressive chromatin, and epigenetic dosage analyses of human beta cells have associated differential EZH2-dependent a non-intersection pathway component methylation with the emergence of functionally distinct beta cell subtypes that differ in diabetes susceptibility. DNMT1 and DNMT3A are, respectively, the principal maintenance and de novo DNA methyltransferases that copy and install cytosine methylation patterns, and studies of shared genetics and islet chromatin organization in Type 2 diabetes have implicated altered DNA methylation at regulatory regions under their control in shaping beta cell and possibly extra-pancreatic phenotypes relevant to glycemic regulation.

Beyond these exemplars, the remaining proteins enriched in chromatin organization can be grouped into several functional clusters. A Polycomb and histone methylation cluster includes EED, EZH1, EHMT1, EHMT2, ASH2L, DPY30, BPTF, ASXL1, EPC2, BMI1 and the chromobox proteins CBX1, CBX2, CBX3, CBX4, CBX5, CBX6 and CBX8; together these factors scaffold, recruit or interpret repressive histone marks such as H3K27me3 and H3K9me2/3, thereby stabilizing long-term transcriptional programs that are remodeled in islet beta cells in the context of diabetes. An ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling and histone chaperone cluster, comprising ACTL6A, ARID2, ARID4A, CHD3, CHD4, ASF1A, CHAF1A, DEK, DDX21 and DMAP1, modulates nucleosome positioning and histone exchange to adjust accessibility of regulatory DNA, a process that large-scale pancreatic islet chromatin profiling has shown to differ between non-diabetic and diabetes-prone states. A DNA damage–responsive chromatin modifier cluster—including BRCA1, BARD1, BAP1, BABAM2, BRCC3 and CHEK2—coordinates ubiquitin signaling and repair-associated chromatin remodeling at DNA lesions, aligning with genetic studies that suggest overlap between Type 2 diabetes and cancer susceptibility through shared genome maintenance pathways. A structural chromatin component cluster is formed by the linker histones H1-1, H1-2, H1-4 and H1-5 together with the a non-intersection pathway component family members H2AB1, H2AC1, H2AC12, H2AC14, H2AC16, H2AC20, H2AC21, H2AC25 and H2AC6, whose variant composition influences nucleosome stability and higher-order fiber compaction in islet and non-islet tissues. Finally, a transcriptional cofactor and regulatory adaptor cluster, containing GATA3, EYA1, EYA2, GATAD2A, GATAD2B, EMSY and EP400, connects chromatin remodeling complexes to sequence-specific transcription factors, providing additional routes by which diabetes risk variants can rewire regulatory circuits uncovered by single-cell and 3D chromatin studies.

Taken together, enrichment of Type 2 diabetes mellitus proteins in chromatin organization suggests that inherited and acquired risk for disease is at least partly mediated through altered higher-order genome architecture and its impact on beta cell and other metabolic cell transcriptional programs. Within this pathway, EP300, CTCF and EZH2 appear to be key drivers of the association, integrating enhancer acetylation, genome topology and Polycomb-mediated repression at diabetes-linked regulatory regions. The coordinated actions of DNMT1 and DNMT3A with these factors further point to combined histone and DNA methylation mechanisms in establishing chromatin states associated with distinct beta cell subtypes and disease susceptibility. Well-documented interactions such as the BRCA1–BARD1 complex and the assembly of EZH2 with EED and a non-intersection pathway component proteins in Polycomb repressive complexes underscore that multi-protein chromatin assemblies, rather than single factors, likely mediate much of the observed genetic and epigenetic contribution of this pathway to Type 2 diabetes mellitus.

paragraphs: 53 submitted Type 2 diabetes mellitus-associated proteins were significantly enriched in heterochromatin organization (GO:0070828).

Among the DNA methylation regulators enriched in this term, DNMT1, DNMT3A and UHRF1 provide a strong link between heterochromatin maintenance and Type 2 diabetes mellitus. DNMT1 maintains CpG methylation during replication and is recruited to heterochromatin through UHRF1, and altered DNMT1 activity has been reported in insulin-responsive tissues in Type 2 diabetes mellitus in parallel with changes in methylation at metabolic genes. DNMT3A deposits de novo DNA methylation that helps establish repressive chromatin domains, and genetic and epigenetic variation at DNMT3A has been implicated in susceptibility to Type 2 diabetes mellitus and in β-cell functional decline, suggesting that aberrant DNA methylation dynamics contribute to disease-related transcriptional reprogramming within heterochromatic regions.

Core Polycomb repressive complex 2 components EZH2, EED and SUZ12 are also enriched in this pathway and connect histone methylation mediated heterochromatin to Type 2 diabetes mellitus. EZH2 catalyzes a non-intersection pathway component trimethylation, a hallmark of facultative heterochromatin, and altered EZH2 expression has been associated with impaired β-cell proliferation and with transcriptional repression of insulin secretory machinery in diabetic settings. The scaffolding subunits EED and SUZ12 stabilize EZH2 on chromatin and help propagate H3K27me3-enriched domains, and changes in Polycomb-dependent repression in adipose and hepatic tissue in Type 2 diabetes mellitus point to a role for this complex in locking in maladaptive metabolic gene expression states within heterochromatinized loci.

Histone deacetylation and sirtuin-mediated chromatin regulation are represented by SIRT6 together with HDAC1 and HDAC2, providing another route by which heterochromatin organization intersects with Type 2 diabetes mellitus. SIRT6 is a chromatin-bound deacetylase that reinforces repressive chromatin and has been shown to modulate glucose and lipid metabolism; perturbation of SIRT6-dependent chromatin silencing is linked to insulin resistance and abnormal hepatic gluconeogenic gene expression in Type 2 diabetes mellitus. HDAC1 and HDAC2 participate in large co-repressor complexes that deacetylate histones within heterochromatin, and altered HDAC1/2 activity in diabetic β cells and vascular tissue has been associated with dysregulated inflammatory and metabolic gene programs that are normally restrained in compact chromatin domains.

Additional heterochromatin architectural factors with documented links to Type 2 diabetes mellitus include HMGA2, BRCA1 and BMI1. HMGA2 is a non-histone chromatin protein that bends DNA and promotes formation of compact chromatin structures, and genetic variation and expression changes in HMGA2 have been associated with obesity and insulin resistance that commonly co-occur with Type 2 diabetes mellitus, implicating HMGA2-dependent chromatin architecture in adipocyte and islet dysfunction. BRCA1 contributes to the integrity of heterochromatin at DNA damage sites, and impaired BRCA1 function has been reported in diabetic tissues in association with heightened oxidative stress and genomic instability that may secondarily disrupt chromatin compartmentalization. The Polycomb protein BMI1, already noted in earlier pathways, is a key organizer of repressive chromatin at cell-cycle and stress-response genes, and its dysregulation in the diabetic milieu has been linked to impaired β-cell self-renewal and long-term maintenance of heterochromatinized gene networks.

The remaining proteins enriched in heterochromatin organization fall into several functional clusters that collectively support chromatin compaction and gene silencing. A Polycomb and a non-intersection pathway component methylation cluster, comprising BMI1, CBX1, CBX3, CBX5, PCGF3, PCGF5, EED, JARID2, SUZ12 and EZH1, contains canonical a non-intersection pathway component and a non-intersection pathway component components and a non-intersection pathway component family readers that recognize repressive histone marks to nucleate and stabilize heterochromatin. A histone methylation cluster including EHMT1, EHMT2, SUV39H1, SETDB1, KMT2A, KMT2D and RRP8 contributes a non-intersection pathway component and other lysine methyltransferase activities that generate binding platforms for CBX1/CBX3/CBX5 and promote spread of silent chromatin. A histone acetylation and deacetylation cluster, with HAT1, HDAC1, HDAC2, HDAC8 and SIN3A, regulates nucleosomal acetylation states during replication-coupled chromatin assembly and within mature heterochromatin, reinforcing repression in metabolic and stress-response loci that are altered in Type 2 diabetes mellitus. A histone variant and chromatin compaction cluster encompassing H2AB1, H2AC1, H2AC12, H2AC14, H2AC16, H2AC20, H2AC21, H2AC25, H2AC6, H2AC7, H2AJ, H2AX, H2AZ1, H2AZ2, MACROH2A1 and MACROH2A2 contributes specialized histone a non-intersection pathway component isoforms that mark constitutive heterochromatin, DNA damage foci and metabolically responsive chromatin compartments. Finally, a chromatin architecture and DNA repair-linked cluster including CTCF, LMNB1, SMARCA5, MBD3, BAP1, BRCA1, RIF1, TEX15 and FKBP6 comprises boundary elements, nuclear lamina components, ATP-dependent remodelers, methyl-CpG readers and repair-associated factors that together shape higher-order heterochromatin domains whose perturbation has been observed in diabetic cells.

Overall, enrichment of heterochromatin organization indicates that Type 2 diabetes mellitus is characterized by coordinated changes in the enzymes and structural proteins that build and maintain compact chromatin, with consequences for long-term silencing of metabolic and stress-response genes. DNMT1, EZH2 and SIRT6 appear to be key drivers of this association, linking DNA methylation, Polycomb-mediated histone methylation and deacetylase-dependent chromatin compaction to altered transcriptional programs in diabetic tissues. Well-established interactions among the proteins listed for this record, such as the DNMT1–UHRF1 DNA methylation maintenance complex, the a non-intersection pathway component assembly of EZH2 with EED, SUZ12 and JARID2, a non-intersection pathway component complexes containing BMI1 with a non-intersection pathway component proteins and CBX1/CBX3/CBX5, and SIN3A-containing complexes with HDAC1/HDAC2, suggest that multi-protein chromatin modules rather than isolated factors underlie the observed enrichment. These findings support the view that stable reconfiguration of heterochromatin is an integral component of Type 2 diabetes mellitus pathophysiology and a potential source of durable epigenetic memory of the diabetic state.
